title: Female Team-Sport Athletes' Physical Fitness and Jump Performance Kinematics After Plyometric Jump Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plyometric jump training (PJT) can improve athletes' physical fitness across a range of sports and populations. Nonetheless, the role of PJT in adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics remains unclear, particularly given the increasing number of published, heterogeneous studies.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to first examine the effectiveness of PJT in improving physical fitness and jump-performance kinematics in adult female team-sport athletes, and second, to provide evidence-based recommendations for PJT prescription for this population.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO databases up to March 2026. The included studies recruited healthy female team-sport athletes (mean age: ≥ 18 years), incorporated a PJT programme ≥ 2 weeks in duration, included comparator groups, and assessed athletes' physical fitness, jump performance, and/or kinematics. The risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Hedges' g effect sizes (ES) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) were reported using a random-effects model for meta-analyses. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the participant characteristics (height, body mass, sport) and PJT programming variables (duration, frequency, total sessions, weekly total jumps). The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Thirty-one articles were included (n = 609 participants), and 25 were meta-analysed. Two studies were categorised with high RoB (≤ 3 points), 20 studies achieved moderate RoB (4-5 points), and 9 studies achieved low RoB (≥ 6 points). Compared to controls, PJT improved countermovement jump (CMJ) height (ES = 0.550, p < 0.001), CMJ peak concentric velocity (ES = 0.623, p = 0.011), drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) (ES = 0.926, p = 0.001), DJ height (ES = 0.721, p = 0.002), 10 m sprint time (ES = 0.712, p = 0.032), 20 m sprint time (ES = 0.709, p < 0.001), 30 m sprint time (ES = 1.018, p = 0.001), non-linear (agility) Illinois test time (ES = 1.225, p < 0.001) and T test sprint time (ES = 0.965, p < 0.001). Compared to PJT ≤ 6 weeks, longer interventions favoured DJ RSI (p = 0.008), 10 m sprint time (p = 0.001), and Illinois agility test time (p < 0.001). Impact of heterogeneity (I2) remained low (≤ 0.06%) in five analyses and moderate in the other four analyses (≤ 73.1%). The certainty of evidence was considered low to moderate for the study outcomes. Two studies reported that a total of three participants possibly sustained an injury during PJT.
CONCLUSIONS: Adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics improved after PJT when compared to the control condition, including CMJ height, CMJ peak concentric velocity, DJ RSI, linear sprint speed, and non-linear (agility) sprint speed. The improvements were particularly notable with longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks).

title: Quadriceps and hamstring tendon autografts show similar clinical outcomes but distinct strength-recovery profiles after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A meta-analysis.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Graft choice remains a central controversy in primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Quadriceps tendon (QT) and hamstring tendon (HT) autografts may provided similar clinical outcomes but differ in donor-site morbidity and postoperative strength recovery.
OBJECTIVE: To determine whether QT and HT autografts differ in patient-reported outcomes, knee stability, functional performance, strength recovery, donor-site morbidity, and safety after primary ACLR.
EVIDENCE REVIEW: PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from inception to March 17, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) directly comparing QT and HT autografts. The protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD420261340928). Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. No external funding was received.
FINDINGS: Fifteen RCTs involving 936 participants were included, with 470 participants receiving QT autografts and 466 receiving HT autografts. Mean ages ranged from 18.7 to 32.7 years, and most studies reported follow-up at 12 or 24 months. At 24 months, no statistically significant differences were detected between QT and HT autografts in IKDC score (MD = -1.19; 95% CI, -3.84 to 1.47; p = 0.38), Lysholm score (MD = 1.42; 95% CI, -0.60 to 3.45; p = 0.17), or Tegner score (MD = -0.15; 95% CI, -0.70 to 0.39; p = 0.58). At the final available follow-up, graft failure occurred in 12 of 265 participants (4.5%) in the QT group and 11 of 261 participants (4.2%) in the HT group, without a statistically significant difference (RR = 1.11; 95% CI, 0.49 to 2.48; p = 0.81). Overall adverse events also showed no statistically significant difference (RR = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.45 to 1.11; p = 0.13). QT autografts were associated with lower donor-site morbidity scores at 24 months (MD = -4.62; 95% CI, -9.21 to -0.03; p = 0.048), although this secondary finding was based on two trials. Knee stability, range of motion, return-to-sport, and hop-test outcomes showed no consistent differences. At 12 months, HT autografts were associated with relatively greater quadriceps strength symmetry, whereas QT autografts were associated with relatively greater hamstring strength symmetry and higher hamstring-to-quadriceps (H/Q) strength ratios.
- CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: QT and HT autografts produced similar patient-reported, stability, return-to-sport, and safety outcomes after primary ACLR but demonstrated distinct graft-specific strength-recovery profiles. These findings support individualized graft selection rather than consistent clinical superiority of either graft.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, systematic review, and meta-analysis of RCTs.

title: Effectiveness of Digital Health Interventions on Rehabilitation Outcomes in Patients After Total Knee Arthroplasty: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is the most effective treatment for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, but some patients continue to experience persistent postoperative pain, stiffness, and impaired functional recovery. Digital health interventions are increasingly used in rehabilitation after TKA, but their comparative effectiveness remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different digital health interventions on rehabilitation outcomes in patients after TKA and to compare and rank these interventions in terms of pain relief, active knee flexion range of motion (ROM), and knee function to provide evidence for selecting optimal rehabilitation strategies.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Google Scholar, Scopus, CINAHL, MEDLINE (via OvidSP), CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) meeting the inclusion criteria. The RoB 2 tool (Risk of Bias 2; Cochrane) was used to assess risk of bias, and the confidence in network meta-analysis (CINeMA) framework was used to evaluate certainty of evidence. Traditional meta-analysis and network meta-analysis (NMA) were performed using Stata (version 17.0; StataCorp LLC). A random-effects model (DerSimonian-Laird method for estimating τ²) was consistently used across all analyses. For outcomes measured with the same or convertible scales, mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were used to pool effect sizes. Surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values were calculated to summarize the ranking probabilities.
RESULTS: A total of 36 RCTs involving 3067 patients after TKA were included. NMA results showed that compared with conventional rehabilitation (CR), for active flexion ROM, rehabilitation robot (RR; MD 8.96, 95% CI 5.86-12.05), mobile app-based telerehabilitation (MAT; MD 6.36, 95% CI 2.81-9.91), and virtual reality (VR; MD 5.92, 95% CI 2.94-8.90) were significantly superior to CR; for the Hospital for Special Surgery knee score, VR (MD 9.53, 95% CI 5.18-13.88), intelligent rehabilitation system-based telerehabilitation (MD 6.90, 95% CI 2.35-11.44), and RR (MD 5.32, 95% CI 1.61-9.04) were significantly superior to CR; for pain, RR and MAT had relatively high ranking probabilities, but the 95% CIs of most comparisons included 0; for the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index and Timed Up and Go test, only internet videoconference-based telerehabilitation and VR-based telerehabilitation, respectively, were significantly superior to CR. The certainty of evidence for most comparisons was low or very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Digital health interventions may improve pain, active knee flexion ROM, and knee function in patients after TKA. In the SUCRA ranking, RR, VR, and MAT showed favorable ranking probabilities; however, because the network was predominantly star-shaped and the rankings were derived largely from indirect comparisons, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive. Further high-quality studies with direct head-to-head comparisons are needed.

title: Neurocognitive Alterations Manifested as Reaction Time Deficits Following ACL Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is associated with changes in cognitive-motor processing that may persist beyond physical recovery and are not fully identified by conventional physical performance assessments.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate neurocognitive function as expressed through cognitive-motor performance following ACLR compared with healthy individuals, with particular emphasis on reaction time and higher-order cognitive outcomes.
METHODS: Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase) were searched from inception to December 2025. Eligibility criteria included observational studies on cognitive-motor outcomes in individuals from ACLR recovery and healthy controls. Data extraction followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools. Random-effects models were used to calculate standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2, subgroup analyses and publication bias evaluations.
RESULTS: Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participants Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participantswere included. Neurocognitive performance showed a significant impairment in reaction time from ACLR recovery with a moderate effect size (standardized mean difference = 0.56, 95% confidence interval 0.41-0.71, p < 0.001) and high heterogeneity (I2 = 78%). In contrast, pooled analyses showed no statistically significant differences for error rate, accuracy, visual memory, or visual motor speed.
CONCLUSIONS: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with persistent reaction time deficits, whereas pooled analyses of error rate, accuracy, visual memory, and visual motor speed did not demonstrate statistically significant differences compared with healthy controls. This pattern suggests selective impairment in the temporal efficiency of cognitive-motor processing rather than generalized cognitive dysfunction. Reaction time may represent a potential marker of altered cognitive-motor processing following ACLR; however, prospective studies are needed to determine its prognostic value and clinical utility for post-ACLR assessment and return-to-sport decision making.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation Versus Blood Flow Restriction Alone: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Blood flow restriction (BFR) training is increasingly combined with neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) in musculoskeletal rehabilitation to augment strength and hypertrophy, but whether NMES adds benefit beyond BFR alone remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared combined BFR + NMES with BFR alone for muscle strength, muscle morphology (mass, thickness, cross-sectional area), neuromuscular activation, and functional performance. Methods: Randomized trials comparing simultaneous BFR + NMES with BFR alone were eligible. MEDLINE via PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Google Scholar were searched from inception through 15 September 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data; risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE. Random-effects meta-analysis was restricted to independent parallel-group comparisons; crossover and limb-randomized results were pooled only when paired effect estimates and variances were available, otherwise synthesized narratively. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251076162). Results: Five randomized trials involving 174 participants were included. The studies represented healthy-participant training, experimental limb disuse, acute physiological responses, and low-load training in football players with knee osteoarthritis. Quantitative synthesis of torque-based strength found no clear difference between BFR + NMES and BFR alone (MD -41.78 Nm, 95% CI -396.68 to 313.12; p = 0.375; 2 trials, 52 participants), with substantial statistical heterogeneity. Cross-sectional area and rectus femoris EMG RMS were each reported by only two trials and were synthesized narratively. Certainty of evidence was very low across all outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence does not establish a consistent additional benefit of adding NMES to BFR. The pooled torque-based estimate is exploratory because of the small evidence base, substantial statistical heterogeneity, imprecision, and differences in clinical context and outcome measurement. A possible effect on preserving muscle mass during short-term experimental disuse remains preliminary. None of the included trials directly investigated BFR + NMES following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), and its effectiveness in this population remains undetermined.

title: Network meta-analysis of the efficacy of different exercise therapies in patients with knee osteoarthritis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability in the elderly and a growing social burden due to aging and increasing obesity rates. This study aims to investigate the effects of different exercise modalities on pain, physical function, stiffness, and muscle strength in patients with KOA.
METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and EBSCO databases for randomized controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of exercise therapy for KOA from January 2000 to 16 August 2025, followed by an updated search through 28 March 2026. No additional eligible studies were identified in the updated search. In total, 51 studies involving 3,045 participants (71.7% female; study-group mean ages ranged from 50.3 to 74.4 years) were included. The studies were conducted in 14 countries across Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania. A network meta-analysis was performed using Stata 16.0. This systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251177632).
RESULTS: The results showed that mind-body exercise was the most effective in reducing pain (standardized mean differences (SMD) = -1.13, 95% confidence interval (CI) [-1.47 to -0.79], P < 0.001, Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA) = 83%) and improving joint stiffness (SMD = -1.15, 95% CI [-1.59 to -0.70], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 78.5%). Mixed exercise ranked highest in improving knee function (SMD = -1.43, 95% CI [-2.31 to -0.55], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 81.8%), followed by mind-body exercise (SMD = -1.28, 95% CI [-1.64 to -0.93], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 77.4%). Strength training was most effective in enhancing muscle strength (SMD = 0.79, 95% CI [0.470-1.12], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 79.1%).
CONCLUSION: Mind-body exercise appeared to be the most favorable option for reducing pain and stiffness in patients with knee osteoarthritis, whereas strength training appeared to be the most beneficial for improving muscle strength. These findings may help inform individualized exercise prescription, but should be interpreted cautiously given the uncertainty and limitations of the available evidence.

title: Maximal Aerobic Capacity and Aging in Female Masters Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Maximal aerobic capacity ( V ˙ O2max) represents the highest rate at which the body can use oxygen during intense exercise and is a key determinant of endurance performance. Although age-related declines in V ˙ O2max have been well documented in male individuals, less is known about this trajectory in female Masters athletes, defined as individuals aged 40 years or older who often engage in lifelong endurance training.
OBJECTIVE: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify cross-sectional age-related differences in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes.
METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 14 May, 2025 for studies reporting directly measured V ˙ O2max in female Masters endurance athletes aged 40 years or older. Eligible exercise modalities included running, cycling, swimming, and large muscle-mass ergometry, with testing conducted under standard environmental conditions. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using a modified Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled mean V ˙ O2max values were calculated for predefined age groups (40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70 years or older) using a random-effects meta-analysis. Meta-regression was used to estimate the relationship between age and V ˙ O2max.
RESULTS: Sixty-nine studies, including 1903 female Masters athletes, met the inclusion criteria. Pooled mean relative V ˙ O2max was 45 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 43.0-46.8) in athletes aged 40-49 years, 40 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 38.5-41.7) in those aged 50-59 years, 35 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 33.2-37.1) in those aged 60-69 years, and 30 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 27.2-31.8) in athletes aged 70 years or older. Meta-regression demonstrated that each additional year of age was associated with a 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 lower V ˙ O2max (95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.44; P < 0.0001), equivalent to about 11.7% per decade. The association was consistent across testing modalities.
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrates a progressive age-related decrease in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes. Maximal aerobic capacity declines at an average rate of 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 per year after age 40 years, corresponding to approximately 11.7% per decade. This decline is evident across endurance sport disciplines and appears consistent with physiological changes associated with aging despite sustained endurance training. These findings provide female-specific reference values and a quantitative framework for future studies on aerobic capacity trajectories in female athletes.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S2RXZ ).

title: Effectiveness of Adding Neuromuscular Training to Conventional Physiotherapy in Adults with Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is associated with pain, functional limitation and impaired balance. This study investigated whether adding neuromuscular training to conventional physiotherapy provides additional benefit over conventional physiotherapy alone in adults with PFPS. Methods: In this single-blind randomized controlled trial (NCT06407414), 56 adults aged 30-60 years with PFPS were randomized to conventional physiotherapy alone (control) or conventional physiotherapy plus neuromuscular training, each performed three times per week for 12 weeks as a home-based program with physiotherapist follow-up every three weeks. The analysis was per protocol and included the 50 of 56 randomized participants (25 per group) who completed the trial. The primary outcome was the Kujala Patellofemoral Score. Secondary outcomes were pain (Visual Analog Scale, VAS), the 30-Second Chair Stand Test, the Y Balance Test, the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form (IPAQ) and, as an exploratory outcome, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Results: After treatment, the neuromuscular training group had higher Kujala scores (median 77 vs. 65; r = 0.81, 95% CI 0.69-0.89) and lower VAS scores (r = 0.72, 95% CI 0.55-0.83), and performed better on the chair stand test (mean difference 2.60 repetitions, 95% CI 0.88-4.32) and IPAQ-walking; these differences remained significant after Bonferroni correction for 12 comparisons, although for the chair stand test this was not consistent in a supplementary change-score analysis. Y Balance Test values are reported descriptively only, because the groups differed at baseline and the analytical definition of the reported values (stance limb) could not be verified against the original records. Between-group differences in the other IPAQ domains and the PSQI were not significant and were inconclusive. Conclusions: Under the conditions of this trial, adding neuromuscular training to conventional physiotherapy produced greater short-term improvements in pain and function than conventional physiotherapy alone. No conclusion is drawn regarding dynamic balance, and the effect on sleep quality remains uncertain.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Focused Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy for Hemiplegic Shoulder Pain: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of ultrasound-guided focused extracorporeal shock wave therapy (fESWT) for hemiplegic shoulder pain (HSP) in patients with ultrasound-confirmed periarticular soft tissue lesions.
METHODS: This single-center, three-arm randomized controlled trial enrolled 114 patients with HSP, randomly allocated 1:1:1 to sham stimulation, conventional landmark-guided fESWT, or ultrasound-guided fESWT. All groups received standardized conventional rehabilitation. fESWT was delivered twice weekly for four sessions. The primary outcome was resting Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain score at 2 weeks post-treatment. Secondary outcomes included shoulder passive range of motion (PROM), Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer Assessment (U-FMA) score, and lesion-specific ultrasound response rate. Intention-to-treat analysis was applied.
RESULTS: At 3 days post-treatment, both fESWT groups had significantly lower VAS scores than the sham group (P < 0.01), with no difference between active groups. At 2, 4, and 8 weeks, VAS scores followed the gradient: ultrasound-guided group < conventional group < sham group (all P < 0.001). For PROM and U-FMA, both active groups improved more than sham. However, after Bonferroni correction, the difference between ultrasound-guided and conventional fESWT was significant for flexion (P = 0.009) but not for abduction, external rotation, or U-FMA. Ultrasound-guided fESWT achieved the highest response rates for tendinitis and bursitis; no significant between-group differences were found for tendon tears. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSION: fESWT as an adjunct to conventional rehabilitation effectively reduces pain and improves function in patients with HSP and ultrasound-confirmed periarticular lesions. Ultrasound guidance further enhances therapeutic outcomes. Larger multicenter trials are warranted to confirm these findings.

title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up).
RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months.
CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.

title: Psychological interventions for anorexia nervosa in female athletes: A mixed-methods systematic review.
abstract: ObjectiveFemale athletes are at high risk of anorexia nervosa. Current clinical guidelines and psychological treatments are largely based on evidence from the general population, highlighting the need for a tailored review of the evidence. This review addresses two complementary questions: first, what evidence exists regarding the effectiveness of psychological interventions; and second, how do athletes with anorexia nervosa experience psychological treatment and recovery, and what factors may influence these experiences?MethodsA convergent, segregated mixed-methods systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines and the Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251073240). Eight databases were searched up to April 2026. Studies were eligible if they involved adult female athletes aged ≥18 years, had a clinical diagnosis of anorexia nervosa and included a psychological intervention component. Quantitative findings were synthesised narratively using the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis framework, with certainty assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Qualitative findings underwent Joanna Briggs Institute meta-aggregation, with certainty assessed using the Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research approach. The findings were then integrated.ResultsEleven studies involving 153 participants (136 female and 17 male) were included. Most studies were conducted in the United States and used cognitive behavioural therapy as a core intervention. The certainty of evidence was very low across all quantitative outcomes (eating disorder psychopathology, weight restoration and return to sport), although the findings indicated potential for recovery. Qualitative evidence suggested that recovery is influenced by environmental, cultural and multidisciplinary support factors. Three themes illustrated these influences, and the integrated findings provided further insight.ConclusionStandard psychological treatments appear capable of supporting recovery in athletes, although outcomes may be enhanced when treatment delivery incorporates athlete-specific considerations, such as athletic identity, performance motivation, coach involvement and return-to-sport planning. Interventions may be more effective when they incorporate sport-specific cultural competence, performance-framed cognitive restructuring, structured coach involvement and return-to-sport goals. Future research should prioritise athlete-adapted experimental designs with sport-specific outcome measures to strengthen the evidence base.

title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes.
METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used.
RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage.
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

title: Multi-planar patellar hypomobility as a potential contributor to VMO-VL dyssynergy and return to sport limitations following ACL reconstruction in soccer players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patellofemoral hypomobility (PFH) is a frequent yet underestimated complication following anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. PFH induces biomechanical and neuromuscular alterations that impair return to sport (RTS) and accelerate early joint degeneration. However, current evidence describes PFH primarily as an associated factor rather than a direct causal determinant of RTS failure. Therefore, the primary objective of this review is to analyze the correlation between PFH and functional complications during RTS. The study also aims to summarize the available evidence on the relationship between PFH and medium- to long-term clinical outcomes, without implying causal predictions where not supported.
METHODS: A narrative review was conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Web of Science using a Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO)-structured search. No systematic review procedures or pooled quantitative analyses were performed; all numerical data derived from individual studies. Included studies involved athletes aged 18-35 undergoing primary ACL reconstruction with Bone-Patellar Tendon-Bone (BPTB) or Hamstring autografts.
RESULTS: The analysis reveals significant PFH (>25% compared to the contralateral side) in 15-22% of athletes at 6 months, with a peak of 28% in BPTB graft cases. Longitudinal hypomobility correlates with extension deficit, whereas transverse hypomobility is associated with increased anterior knee pain (AKP) in 34% of cases. Data indicate a 12-15% reduction in Countermovement Jump (CMJ) performance and a 3.4-fold higher risk of patellofemoral osteoarthritis (PFOA) within 5 years, although PFH was not directly measured as an independent variable in these studies. Additionally, 25% of athletes with PFH discontinue competitive activity within 36 months after RTS.
CONCLUSIONS: PFH emerges as an important factor associated with postoperative functional limitations. Restricted patellar glide disrupts the vastus medialis obliquus (VMO)/vastus lateralis (VL) synergy, reduces performance, and accelerates cartilage degeneration. Symmetry of patellar kinematics should be considered a relevant parameter for RTS decision-making, while acknowledging that RTS outcomes are multifactorial and not solely determined by PFH.

title: Greater eccentric hamstrings to concentric quadriceps strength ratio at 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with reduced odds of revision within 2 years.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the association between eccentric hamstrings-to-concentric quadriceps strength ratio (mixed hamstrings to quadriceps [HQ]-strength ratio) at 6 months postoperatively and revision anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACL-R) within 2 years of primary surgery. The secondary purpose was to investigate the association between the mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance limb symmetry index (LSI).
METHODS: Data were collected from a local registry at Capio Artro Clinic, Stockholm, Sweden. Patients aged ≥15 years, without concomitant ligament injuries and meniscal resection or repair who underwent primary ACL-R with hamstring tendon autografts between 2005 and 2021 were included. Isokinetic eccentric hamstrings and concentric quadriceps strength were assessed using a Biodex dynamometer 6 months postoperatively. Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg and revision ACL-R were analysed using multivariable logistic regression analysis, presented with odds ratios (ORs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC). Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance LSI were analysed with linear regression.
RESULTS: Of the 3458 patients included, 49.5% were female and the mean age was 28.8 ± 10.4 years. Patients who underwent revision ACL-R within 2 years had lower mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg 6 months postoperatively. After adjustment for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level, each 10-unit increase in the mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg was associated with lower odds of revision ACL-R (OR = 0.81, 95% CI [0.71;0.93], p = 0.003). However, the discriminatory ability was poor (AUC = 0.64). A greater mixed HQ-strength ratio was associated with poorer single-leg hop for distance LSI, adjusted for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level (β = -1.30, 95% CI [-1.51;-1.09], p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The mixed HQ-strength ratio may complement the evaluation of muscle strength recovery after ACL-R. However, its poor discriminatory ability limits its use to identify patients who will undergo revision ACL-R.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Developmental Differences in Muscle, Tendon, and Cartilage Injuries among Elite Badminton Players.
abstract: This study investigated differences in the characteristics of severe muscle, tendon, and cartilage injuries according to injury timing and post-injury management among elite badminton players. A retrospective interview study was conducted involving 126 badminton players aged 19 to 24 years. A total of 87 severe injury cases reported by 73 athletes were analyzed, with some athletes contributing more than one case. Injuries were classified according to timing into the secondary school group (n=33) and the post-secondary group (n=54). Injury characteristics and post-injury management were compared using chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, with effect sizes. Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals examined associations with injury timing. Compared with the secondary school group, the post-secondary group had higher odds of lower limb muscle injuries (odds ratio=6.00, 95% confidence interval=1.85-19.47, p=0.003) and smash/stroke-related injuries (odds ratio=5.43, 95% confidence interval=1.15-25.66, p=0.033), whereas the post-secondary group had lower odds of lower limb tendinopathies (odds ratio=0.21, 95% confidence interval=0.08-0.55, p=0.001). These findings suggest that severe injury characteristics may differ according to the timing of injury occurrence, despite no significant between-group differences in post-injury management, and may help inform potential injury prevention priorities based on the observed injury patterns.

title: Outcomes of open and endoscopic excision of a symptomatic os trigonum in athletes: a systematic review with exploratory analysis of prognostic factors.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: A symptomatic os trigonum causes posterior ankle impingement in athletes and is excised when conservative treatment fails. Previous syntheses have pooled mean outcomes across mixed populations, and poor outcomes have not been defined consistently.
METHODS: Six databases were searched for open or endoscopic os trigonum excision in athletes, following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM. Techniques were compared within comparative studies, with supplementary pooling. A composite poor-outcome profile and eight candidate factors were examined at study-arm level.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies (17 arms, 440 participants) were included. Failure to return to prior level was uncommon (9 of 438; 0-6.2% by arm). In the randomised trial, return to prior sport level was 4.4 weeks faster after endoscopic excision (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.7-6.1); pooling two further non-randomised studies with imputed SDs gave 4.9 weeks (95% CI 3.3-6.6). Trial complications occurred in 1 of 26 endoscopic and 6 of 26 open patients (odds ratio 7.50, 95% CI 0.83-67.49); the two-study pooled odds ratio was 5.59 (95% CI 1.10-28.35) from 10 events. Both nerve injuries described as permanent followed open surgery. The composite depended on arm size and threshold choice, and five of eight candidate factors could not be tested.
CONCLUSION: Poor outcomes are uncommon after either approach. Low-certainty evidence suggests faster return to sport after endoscopic excision; complication evidence is of very low certainty, though no nerve injury described as permanent followed endoscopic excision. A consensus definition of return to sport is needed.

title: Temporal dynamics of the repeated bout effect on exercise-induced muscle damage: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The repeated bout effect (RBE) confers protection against exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD). However, the temporal profile of this protective response both across post-exercise recovery and across different intervention-to-damage intervals remains poorly defined. This three-level meta-analysis aimed to quantify the time-course of RBE protective effects and to characterize potential temporal windows for intervention and measurement.
METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus (inception to June 2025) identified 35 eligible studies. Three outcome measures, maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), and creatine kinase (CK), were analyzed using three-level random-effects models. Effect sizes (Hedges' g) were stratified by post-exercise measurement time (24, 48, 72, and 96 h) and intervention interval (<1 week, 1-2 weeks, 2-3 weeks, and >3 weeks).
RESULTS: RBE significantly protected MVC (overall g = 1.18, 95% CI: 0.91-1.45) and reduced DOMS (g = -1.37, 95% CI: -1.70 to -1.05) and CK (g = -0.91, 95% CI: -1.33 to -0.50). Time-stratified analyses revealed distinct temporal patterns. MVC and DOMS showed their largest observed protective estimates at 72 h post-damage (g = 1.47 and -1.65, respectively), whereas CK showed its largest observed protective estimate at 96 h (g = -1.53). Direct comparisons accounting for within-study dependence showed a larger MVC estimate at 72 h than at 48 h and a more protective CK estimate at 48 h than at 24 h. Subgroup analyses revealed outcome-specific interval patterns, with pooled protective effects for MVC and DOMS numerically smallest in magnitude in the 2-3-week subgroup at all four assessed time points.
CONCLUSION: RBE-related protection showed time-dependent patterns across outcomes. Among the assessed time points, pooled protective effects were largest in magnitude at 72 h for functional (MVC) and perceptual (DOMS) outcomes, whereas biochemical (CK) effects increased progressively in magnitude through 96 h. The 2-3-week interval was characterized by numerically weaker pooled protective effects for MVC and DOMS. These findings provide an evidence-informed temporal framework for optimizing preconditioning and recovery-monitoring strategies in athletic training.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: STUDY00004409).

title: Sex-Equitable Machine Learning Prediction of Ankle Reinjury in Individuals with Chronic Ankle Instability: A 2-Year Prospective Cohort Study with Fairness Audit.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI) face a 2-year reinjury rate approaching 50%, but individualized prediction models that quantify which baseline impairments predict subsequent reinjury within an established CAI cohort remain scarce, and existing prediction models for ankle injury have not assessed sex-related fairness. The aim was to develop and internally validate sex-equitable machine learning (ML) models predicting 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, identify the most influential baseline prognostic markers, and audit sex-stratified model performance.
METHODS: One hundred physically active individuals (50 male, 50 female) with CAI (mean age 21.8 ± 2.3 years) were recruited from a university population between February 2017 and February 2018 and prospectively followed for 2 years; 96 (49 male, 47 female) with at least one follow-up response were retained for analysis (41 reinjury events, 43% reinjury rate). Fourteen baseline predictors spanning demographic, anthropometric, injury-history, patient-reported, biomechanical, postural-control, and functional-performance domains were collected. Six algorithms were trained with nested cross-validation: an unpenalized logistic regression baseline and five ML algorithms (Elastic Net, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM). Predictive contribution of each feature was quantified using Shapley additive explanations and partial-dependence plots. A pre-specified fairness audit compared single global and sex-specific Youden thresholds derived out-of-fold using the equalized-odds gap and disproportionate-impact ratio.
RESULTS: All algorithms achieved area under the curve (AUC) values above 0.70; Elastic Net was selected as the primary model (AUC = 0.807, 95% CI 0.714-0.893; calibration slope = 1.015). Sex, arch height index, previous sprains, dorsiflexion range of motion, and Biodex Overall Stability Index consistently emerged as the most influential prognostic markers. Within-sex discrimination was comparable between males and females, but a single global threshold produced an equalized-odds gap of 0.384 that was reduced by 57% (to 0.164) through sex-specific thresholding without retraining the model.
CONCLUSIONS: ML models with a fairness-audited threshold strategy predicted 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, reducing the equalized-odds gap by 57%, though the disproportionate-impact ratio (0.683) remained below the 0.80 benchmark. External validation is required before clinical deployment.

title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

title: Dose-response relationship between training volume and outcomes for hip osteoarthritis: Exploratory study from The Hip Booster Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To explore associations between training volume and changes in patient-reported hip pain and physical function, performance-based function, and muscle power in patients with hip osteoarthritis.
DESIGN: Exploratory cohort study with data from The HipBooster Trial.
SETTING: Five hospitals and 10 physiotherapy clinics across Denmark.
PARTICIPANTS: 144 of 160 patients who had complete training and outcome data.
INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized to 12 weeks of twice-weekly progressive resistance training (PRT) or neuromuscular exercise (NEMEX).
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Hip disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) pain and Activities of Daily Living (ADL), 30-s chair stand test (30s-CST), and leg extensor power (LEP) assessed at baseline and post-intervention.
RESULTS: In the PRT group, each 10 000 kg increase in total training volume across 24 sessions was associated with an increase of 1.13 (95% CI: -0.01; 2.26) points for HOOS pain, 1.33 (95% CI: 0.26; 2.39) for HOOS ADL, 0.12 (95% CI: -0.10; 0.33) repetitions in the 30s-CST, and 2.37 (95% CI: -0.68; 5.43) watts in LEP. In the NEMEX group, each 2000 repetitions increase in total training volume was associated with an increase of 1.12 (95% CI: -0.61; 2.85) points for HOOS pain, 1.92 (95% CI: 0.13; 3.70) for HOOS ADL, 0.31 (95% CI: -0.08; 0.70) repetitions in the 30s-CST, and -1.25 (95% CI: -5.92; 3.43) watts in LEP.
CONCLUSION: Greater total training volume seems associated with slightly greater improvements in pain and physical function in hip osteoarthritis. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, given the exploratory nature of the study.

title: Arthroscopic Stabilization Reduces Recurrence but May Delay Return to Sport After First-Time Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocation in Elite Male Athletes: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management for first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation in adult athletes, with a focus on recurrent instability, return-to-play rates, and time to return to play.
METHODS: Five databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Studies comparing arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management in adult athletes (≥18 years) with first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation were included. The primary outcome was recurrent instability. Secondary outcomes included return-to-play rates and time to return to play. A narrative synthesis was performed given the nonrandomized and heterogeneous nature of included studies. Evidence certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation.
RESULTS: Five studies (232 participants: 111 operative, 121 nonoperative) were included. Recurrent instability rates ranged from 3% to 14% in the operative group and 24% to 80% in the nonoperative group. Return-to-play rates were high for both approaches (operative: 93%-100%; nonoperative: 97%-100%). Nonoperative management was associated with earlier return to sport (2.3-5.7 weeks vs 18.7-39.3 weeks for operative management in studies reporting this outcome). All studies involved elite athletes, with female athletes substantially under-represented.
CONCLUSIONS: Arthroscopic stabilization was consistently associated with lower rates of recurrent instability than nonoperative management after first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation but required a longer time to return to play. Nonoperative management enabled an earlier return to play but was associated with higher recurrence. The evidence is limited primarily to male military, collegiate, and professional athletes, restricting generalizability to female, recreational, and broader adult athletic populations.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting.
METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed.
RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown.
METHODS: In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise.
RESULTS: EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: -10.9%, 95%CI: -21.4;-0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: -9.80, 95%CI: -18.3;-1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis.
CONCLUSION: n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

title: Influence of ballistic and conventional resistance training on bone properties in postmenopausal women: A randomised controlled trial.
abstract: High-load conventional resistance training (CRT) is recommended for osteoporosis prevention. Ballistic resistance training (BRT) involves high velocity and impact forces with lower loads. The Resistance Exercise Programme on Risk of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis in Females (REPROOF) study examined effects of BRT and CRT, relative to control (CON) on proximal femur BMD. Healthy postmenopausal women aged 50-70 years were randomised into BRT, CRT or CON groups. BRT and CRT conducted supervised resistance training twice weekly for eight months. In CRT, concentric and eccentric phases each lasted ~2 s at 55-80% of one-repetition maximum (1RM). BRT involved explosive (maximum velocity) concentric movements at 20-50% of 1RM. Proximal femur and lumbar spine BMD were measured by DXA; tibia structure by peripheral QCT. Groups were compared using ANCOVA, adjusting for baseline values. Of 109 women randomised, 82 (63.1 ± 3.7 years; 24.5 ± 3.5 kgm-2; femoral neck T-score -1.1 ± 0.8) completed the study, with 98% adherence. BRT improved total hip BMD (+0.008 [0.001, 0.014] g/cm2; P = 0.02) versus CON. CRT did not affect hip BMD but tibial shaft cortical BMD increased (+4.141 [1.007, 7.274] g/cm2; P = 0.01) and cortical thickness declined relative to CON (-0.07 [-0.13, -0.01] mm; P = 0.03), accompanied by tibial shaft widening. BRT increased total hip and trochanter BMD (P ≤ 0.03) in the subgroup with low BMD. BRT benefitted proximal femur BMD relative to CON, including in the subgroup with low BMD. CRT did not affect hip BMD but caused tibial shaft structural adaptation that may affect strength in bending. BRT based interventions should be further developed and evaluated for osteoporosis prevention.

title: Characterising the Internal and External Load During Warm-Up, Match Play and Training in Soccer Substitutes: A Systematic Scoping Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Shorter match-play exposure for soccer substitutes relative to those who start matches has implications in the days before, during and following match play concerning their training, preparatory and recovery/compensatory practices. Specifically, characterising the internal and external loading of substitute players throughout a weekly microcycle can facilitate evidence-based recommendations aimed at optimising their performance readiness.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic scoping review aimed to map and characterise the internal and external loading associated with warm-up, match play and training in soccer substitutes.
METHODS: Prior to literature searches being conducted, a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) statement was formed. Online database (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science) searches were performed according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) protocols. Studies were eligible if internal or external characteristics of soccer substitutes were measured in training or match-play scenarios. After calibration exercises, two authors independently quality assessed each study, with Cohen's kappa undertaken to assess inter-rater agreement. A scoping review methodology was selected because of the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity across studies, which precluded meaningful meta-analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 5135 studies were identified, 66 of which met study criteria. Substantive inter-rater agreement was observed (κ = 0.939, p < 0.001) during the quality assessment of included studies. Soccer substitutes' body temperature, and thus several aspects of physical performance, may not be maintained at time of pitch entry (body temperature pre-pitch entry ~ 37 °C vs match play > 38 °C). Substitutes may experience lower absolute physical loading during training and match day (e.g. match-day 'top up' activity: ~ 17 min; total distance: ~ 1700 m) but during match play, substitutes typically cover higher relative total distances (~ 109 to ~ 137 m·min-1), high-speed running (~ 9.8 to ~ 13.5 m·min-1) and sprinting distance (~ 3.8 to 5.0 m·min-1) compared with players who started the match. Substitutes playing in the second-half exhibit increased heart rates compared with full-match players (84% vs 81% maximum heart rate); however, this remains lower than the first-half heart rate responses of full-match players (84% vs 86% maximum heart rate).
CONCLUSIONS: This systematic scoping review summarises current evidence and key findings relating to the internal and external characteristics of soccer substitutes during warm-up, match play and training that can be used in practice to inform player welfare and sport science support within these cohorts. Chiefly, during match-day warm-ups, soccer substitutes' body temperature and physical performance responses may not be maintained, despite typical substitute-specific match-day practices being employed. Similarly, soccer substitutes were frequently reported to demonstrate higher relative total distance, high-speed running and sprinting outputs compared with starting players. Further research is needed to better understand performance demands, longitudinal adaptations, contextual influences and female-specific responses in soccer substitutes.

title: Musculoskeletal Health in Elite Athletes With Bilateral Lower Limb Loss: The ADVANCE Cohort Study.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Lower limb (LL) loss can be detrimental to bone and joint health. Exercise improves musculoskeletal outcomes in individuals without LL loss, but with limited investigation after LL loss. The aim is to assess differences in bone and joint health between elite athletes and nonathletes with bilateral LL loss to assess associations between exercise and musculoskeletal health in this population.
DESIGN: ADVANCE (Armed Services Trauma Rehabilitation Outcome) is a longitudinal cohort study involving UK military personnel and veterans who served in Afghanistan.
METHODS: Sixty-four ambulatory participants with bilateral LL loss were included. Seven participants were elite athletes (athlete group; n = 7) and were compared with the remaining participants (nonathlete group, n = 57). The Kellgren-Lawrence score for knee and hip osteoarthritis (OA), femoral neck and lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, International Physical Activity Questionnaire, and 6-minute walk test distance were compared. Outcomes were also compared between the Athlete group and Nonathlete group split by activity level.
RESULTS: Participants were 33.1 ± 4.7 years old and 6.9 ± 1.5 years postinjury. No Athlete group participants had knee OA compared with 51.8% of Nonathlete participants. There was a weak trend for more prevalent hip OA in the Nonathlete group (P = .074); 7.1% Athlete group participants and 30.7% Nonathlete group participants had Kellgren-Lawrence score ≥ 1. Femoral neck BMD was not different between groups, but there was a trend for lower lumbar spine BMD in the Nonathlete group compared with the Athlete group (-0.41 vs 0.57; P = .06). More active nonathletes had better femoral neck t scores than less active nonathletes, P = .03. Neither Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Pain, Symptoms, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, nor 6-minute walk test distance were different between groups.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and active nonathletes with LL loss may have favorable BMD profiles. Athletes with LL loss have lower prevalence of radiographic hip and knee OA. Although not conclusive due to our study design, this suggests that exercise may be associated with beneficial musculoskeletal health outcomes in this population.

title: Five-year outcomes after brace-free versus brace-based rehabilitation following isolated anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft: long-term follow-up of a randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Postoperative knee bracing following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains common practice despite growing evidence questioning its clinical benefit. Previous studies demonstrated that brace-free rehabilitation was noninferior to brace-based rehabilitation one year after isolated ACLR using hamstring tendon autograft; however, its long-term effects remain unknown. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term effects five years after surgery.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients enrolled in a prospective randomized controlled trial conducted between 2016 and 2019 were recontacted approximately five years after isolated primary ACLR with hamstring tendon autograft for a long-term follow-up. In the original trial, 139 patients had been randomized to postoperative rehabilitation without a brace (n = 71) or with a functional knee brace (n = 68). Participants completed several patient-reported outcome measures. Furthermore, a standardized telephone interview was performed. Changes between the one-year and five-year follow-up were analyzed.
RESULTS: Ninety-seven patients participated in the long-term follow-up (n = 45 brace-free group, n = 52 brace group). Mean follow-up was 5.2 ± 1.0 years. No significant differences were observed between groups regarding subjective knee function, activity level, quality of life, rerupture rate, revision surgery, or persistent knee-related complaints at final follow-up. However, there was a significant interaction between treatment group and time for the subjective IKDC score. Patients treated without postoperative bracing showed stable or slightly improved subjective knee function, whereas patients treated with a brace demonstrated a significant decline between one and five years.
DISCUSSION: Brace-free rehabilitation after isolated ACL reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft remains safe and effective more than five years after surgery. Postoperative bracing did not reduce rerupture rates, revision surgery, or long-term functional impairment. Instead, brace-free rehabilitation demonstrated a more favorable longitudinal development of subjective knee function. These findings further question the routine postoperative prescription of rehabilitative knee braces following isolated ACL reconstruction.

title: Web-based rehabilitation after surgical salvage procedures for wrist osteoarthritis: protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Wrist osteoarthritis (OA) is a disabling condition often affecting individuals of working age and frequently resulting from previous trauma. When non-operative management fails, surgical salvage procedures may reduce pain but require structured postoperative rehabilitation. Telerehabilitation has demonstrated comparable outcomes to standard face-to-face rehabilitation in several musculoskeletal conditions; however, evidence following its effectiveness after wrist OA surgery is lacking. This trial aims to evaluate whether a web-based rehabilitation programme is non-inferior to standard, face-to-face rehabilitation following surgical salvage procedures for wrist OA.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This is a prospective, parallel-group, assessor-blinded, randomised controlled non-inferiority trial conducted at a tertiary hand surgery centre. 90 adults undergoing surgical salvage procedures for wrist OA (four-corner fusion, lunocapitate fusion, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid fusion, radioscapholunate fusion or proximal row carpectomy) will be randomised 1:1 to receive either postoperative web-based rehabilitation or standard face-to-face rehabilitation. The primary outcome is the patient-rated wrist evaluation score measured 12 weeks after immobilisation has ended. Secondary outcomes include pain, health-related quality of life, fear of movement, range of motion, grip strength, patient-reported experience, adherence and cost of rehabilitation.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval has been granted by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority in November 2024. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT06814821

title: Clinical Outcomes of Zone I Flexor Digitorum Profundus Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Last 25 Years.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Zone I flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon injuries, at the distal phalanx insertion, generally require surgery. However, outcomes may vary, and multiple surgical techniques have been described. This review sought to evaluate management, rehabilitation, and outcomes following zone I FDP injuries.
METHODS: Using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, a systematic review and meta-analysis was performed. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane were queried for articles concerning zone I FDP injuries since 2000. Patients younger than 18 years of age and revision surgery were excluded. Demographics, strength, range of motion, outcome scores, therapy protocols, and complications were evaluated.
RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria and were stratified by treatment strategy into 31 cohorts comprising 669 fingers. The mean age was 36 years and 25% were women. Injury mechanisms included 348 lacerations (52%) and 234 avulsions (35%); 88 injuries (13%) were unspecified. Primary tenorrhaphy was the most frequently reported treatment (39%), followed by tenorrhaphy with a tie-over button (10%) and bone anchor fixation (10%). The mean time to surgery was 4 days. Range of motion or outcome measures were documented in 12 cohorts (39%) and strength in 10 cohorts (32%). Meta-analysis demonstrated postoperative FDP rupture, revision surgery, and tenolysis rates of 2.0%, 1.0%, and 1.6%, respectively. Lacerations were treated with primary tenorrhaphy more commonly compared with avulsions (59% vs 22%) and had higher revision rates (7.6% vs 1.4%).
CONCLUSIONS: Surgical repair of zone I FDP injuries demonstrates low complication rates and generally favorable outcomes; however, inconsistent reporting of functional outcomes limits meaningful comparison between surgical techniques.

title: Fueling the Modern Endurance Athlete: The High-Carbohydrate Revolution, Exogenous Ketones, and an Evidence-Based Approach for the Sports Medicine Clinician.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Carbohydrate is the principal limiting fuel for prolonged, high-intensity endurance exercise, and consensus guidelines have long capped recommended intake during exercise at approximately 90 g/h. Two developments have challenged and extended contemporary fueling practice: a shift toward carbohydrate intakes of 100 to 150 g/h in elite endurance sport, and widespread commercial availability of exogenous ketone supplements marketed as ergogenic aids. Both have outpaced the clinical evidence and have reached the competitive and recreational athletes who present to sports medicine clinicians.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Narrative review of primary metabolic and performance studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus statements published through mid-2026, identified through PubMed and reference tracing.
STUDY DESIGN: Narrative review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 5.
RESULTS: Multiple-transportable-carbohydrate formulations (glucose plus fructose) raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation above the roughly 1 g/minute ceiling imposed by intestinal glucose transport, providing the mechanistic basis for fueling rates of ≥90 g/h. Ingesting 120 g/h increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, but the best-controlled studies have not demonstrated additional endogenous (liver and muscle) glycogen sparing or a consistent performance advantage, and gastrointestinal tolerability requires deliberate gut training. For exogenous ketones, an influential 2016 study reported altered substrate use and improved time-trial performance. Subsequent trials and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have not confirmed an acute ergogenic effect, and several have documented gastrointestinal distress or impaired performance. The more promising and reproducible signal for ketones lies in postexercise recovery and attenuation of overreaching. Finally, athletes who restrict in-competition and training carbohydrate to pursue leanness risk low energy and carbohydrate availability, the substrate of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).
CONCLUSION: Carbohydrate intake of ≤90 g/h, built through progressive gut training, is supported by consensus guidelines and mechanistic evidence for prolonged, high-intensity endurance events; progression toward 120 g/h is reasonable in selected, well-adapted athletes competing in the longest events, with the understanding that a performance benefit >90 g/h remains unproven. Routine exogenous ketone supplementation for acute performance is not supported by current evidence; a recovery-focused application is plausible and increasingly supported but requires further study. Clinicians should frame both strategies within adequate energy availability to protect long-term athlete health.Strength-of-Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT):B.

title: Anthocyanin-Rich Aronia melanocarpa Supplementation Modulates Intestinal Barrier Biomarkers and Stress-Axis Response in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anthocyanin-rich berries may modulate intestinal barrier-related processes and physiological stress responses, but evidence from human studies remains limited.
METHODS: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 15 elite male rowers (Aronia group, n = 7; placebo group, n = 8). Participants received Aronia melanocarpa supplementation or placebo for eight weeks and performed a standardized 2000-m rowing ergometer test before and after the intervention. Circulating claudin-3 (CLDN-3), lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP), and cortisol concentrations were assessed before exercise, immediately after exercise, and following 1 h of recovery.
RESULTS: A significant Group × Time interaction was observed for CLDN-3 (p = 0.0463). After eight weeks, pre-exercise CLDN-3 concentrations were lower in the Aronia group than in the placebo group (p = 0.0367). Lower pre-exercise LBP concentrations (p = 0.0125) and lower cortisol concentrations at 1 h post-exercise (p = 0.0079) were also observed in the Aronia group compared with placebo. No significant supplementation-specific effect was observed for I-FABP.
CONCLUSIONS: Eight weeks of Aronia melanocarpa supplementation was associated with differences in selected intestinal barrier-related biomarkers and post-exercise cortisol concentrations in elite male rowers. However, these findings were primarily related to specific sampling time points and should not be interpreted as evidence of improved intestinal barrier function. Given the small sample size and potential dietary confounding, the results are preliminary and require confirmation in larger randomized controlled trials.
